Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R$ be open and let
$a:\Omega\to\mathbb R^n$, $c:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$.
The scalar first-order equation

$$u_t(x,t)+a(x,t)\cdot\nabla_x u(x,t)+c(x,t)u(x,t)=f(x,t)$$

is a **linear transport equation**.

Fix $(x_0,t_0)\in\Omega$. A **characteristic through $(x_0,t_0)$** is a
solution $X(\cdot)$ of the ODE

$$X'(s)=a(X(s),s),\qquad X(t_0)=x_0,$$

on an interval containing $t_0$. The corresponding space-time curve is
$s\mapsto (X(s),s)$. If these initial-value problems have unique solutions for
varying initial data, write $X(s;t_0,x_0)$ for the solution through
$(x_0,t_0)$. The resulting maps $x_0\mapsto X(s;t_0,x_0)$, on the domains
where they are defined, form the **characteristic flow** of the transport
field. Without uniqueness there are characteristics, but no single-valued
characteristic flow.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

A **smooth hybrid ODE system** on a finite horizon $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$ and positive integer state dimension $d\ge1$, consists of a finite mode set $M$, an open state-time domain $D_m\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ and a $C^1$ vector field $f_m:D_m\to\mathbb R^d$ for each $m\in M$, a finite set of directed transitions $(m,n)$, and for each transition a $C^1$ scalar guard $g_{mn}:D_m\to\mathbb R$, a declared crossing orientation $\sigma_{mn}\in\{-1,+1\}$, and a $C^1$ reset map $R_{mn}:U_{mn}\to\mathbb R^d$ on an open neighborhood $U_{mn}\subseteq D_m$ of the guard zero set, satisfying $(t,R_{mn}(t,x))\in D_n$ for every $(t,x)\in U_{mn}$. Here $C^1$ has the meaning in [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. In mode $m$, a trajectory is a solution of the first-order initial-value problem $y'=f_m(t,y)$ in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. It follows that mode only until the selected event time.

An **event time** for transition $(m,n)$ is a time $\tau$ at which $g_{mn}(\tau,y(\tau))=0$ and the guard crosses in its declared direction, meaning $\sigma_{mn}\frac{d}{dt}g_{mn}(t,y(t))|_{t=\tau}>0$. It is **transverse** with margin $\nu>0$ on a bracket when $\sigma_{mn}\frac{d}{dt}g_{mn}(t,y(t))\ge\nu$ throughout that bracket. At an event, the state changes from $y(\tau^-)$ to $R_{mn}(\tau,y(\tau^-))$ and the mode changes from $m$ to $n$. A **deterministic event-priority rule** is a fixed total order on the finite outgoing transition set of each mode; if several enabled guards vanish at exactly the same first time, the least transition in that order is selected.

A hybrid trajectory has a **finite separated event list** on $[0,T]$ when it has finitely many event times $0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_N<T$ and some $\delta>0$ with $\tau_{j+1}-\tau_j\ge\delta$ for each adjacent pair. The definition does not assert that a solution exists, that an event is detected, or that the event list is finite. Those are separate hypotheses or conclusions.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_d>0$, and let $N_1,\ldots,N_d\ge1$ be integers. The periodic rectangular box is
$$\mathbb T^d_{\ell}:=\mathbb R^d/(\ell_1\mathbb Z\times\cdots\times\ell_d\mathbb Z).$$
Set $h_j:=\ell_j/N_j$. Its uniform tensor grid has nodes $x_{\boldsymbol i}=(i_1h_1,\ldots,i_dh_d)$, indexed by $0\le i_j<N_j$, with indices understood modulo $N_j$.

For node data $V_{\boldsymbol i}$ and a lift $x\in\mathbb R^d$ of a point on the torus, define
$$q_j:=\left\lfloor x_j/h_j\right\rfloor,\qquad \theta_j:=x_j/h_j-q_j\in[0,1),$$
and for $\boldsymbol\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^d$ define
$$w_{\boldsymbol\epsilon}(x):=\prod_{j=1}^d\theta_j^{\epsilon_j}(1-\theta_j)^{1-\epsilon_j}.$$
The tensor-product multilinear interpolant is
$$\mathcal I_hV(x):=\sum_{\boldsymbol\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^d}w_{\boldsymbol\epsilon}(x)V_{([q_1+\epsilon_1]_{N_1},\ldots,[q_d+\epsilon_d]_{N_d})},$$
where $[k]_N$ is the residue in $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. The formula is unchanged when a period $\ell_j$ is added to $x_j$, so it defines an interpolant on $\mathbb T^d_{\ell}$. If $N_j=1$, the two corner indices in that coordinate coincide; the formula still gives the same node value.

For a continuous periodic function $v$, $\mathcal I_hv$ means the interpolant of its grid samples. Put $h:=\max_jh_j$.

derivations.claim: Each factor $\theta_j$ and $1-\theta_j$ is nonnegative, so every $w_{\boldsymbol\epsilon}(x)\ge0$. Summing over all binary vectors factorizes as $\sum_{\boldsymbol\epsilon}w_{\boldsymbol\epsilon}(x)=\prod_{j=1}^d((1-\theta_j)+\theta_j)=1$. Thus $\mathcal I_hV(x)$ is a convex combination of its corner data, even when wrapping makes two corner indices coincide.

If $V_{\boldsymbol i}\ge0$ at every node, each summand in the interpolant is nonnegative, so its value is nonnegative; the same convex-combination identity bounds it by the minimum and maximum corner data.

At each $x$, [F1] and the triangle inequality give $|\mathcal I_hV(x)-\mathcal I_hW(x)|\le\sum_{\boldsymbol\epsilon}w_{\boldsymbol\epsilon}(x)|V_{\boldsymbol i(\boldsymbol\epsilon)}-W_{\boldsymbol i(\boldsymbol\epsilon)}|\le\|V-W\|_{\ell^\infty}\sum_{\boldsymbol\epsilon}w_{\boldsymbol\epsilon}(x)=\|V-W\|_{\ell^\infty}$. Taking the supremum over $x$ proves the stated contraction; no estimate in this argument uses the displacement size.

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, $\ell_j>0$, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $[0,T]$. Suppose $b:J\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is $C^1$ and periodic in $x_j$ with period $\ell_j$ for every $j$. Choose a compact interval $K\subset J$ with $[0,T]\subset\operatorname{int}K$, and put $M_K:=\sup_{K\times[0,\ell_1]\times\cdots\times[0,\ell_d]}\|b\|_2$. For every $s\in[0,T]$ and $x\in\mathbb R^d$, there is a unique solution $X(\cdot;s,x)$ of
$$X'(t)=b(t,X(t)),\qquad X(s;s,x)=x,$$
on the whole interval $[0,T]$. The lifted flow is periodic-equivariant:
$$X(t;s,x+\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell)=X(t;s,x)+\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell\qquad(\boldsymbol k\in\mathbb Z^d),$$
where $\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell=(k_1\ell_1,\ldots,k_d\ell_d)$. If $M_T:=\sup_{[0,T]\times[0,\ell_1]\times\cdots\times[0,\ell_d]}\|b\|_2$, then
$$\|X(t;s,x)-x\|_2\le M_T|t-s|\qquad(t\in[0,T]).$$
Thus each characteristic stays in a compact tube $[0,T]\times\overline B(x,M_TT+1)$.

Let $a$ be $C^1$ on an open neighborhood of the graph of a characteristic
$X(\cdot;\xi_0)$ solving

$$X'(t)=a(X(t),t),\qquad X(t_0;\xi_0)=\xi_0,$$

on a compact interval $I$ containing $t_0$. Then, after shrinking to a
neighborhood $U_0$ of $\xi_0$, every initial point $\xi\in U_0$ determines a
characteristic $X(\cdot;\xi)$ on the same interval $I$, the map
$(t,\xi)\mapsto X(t;\xi)$ is continuous on $I\times U_0$, and for each
$t\in I$ the map $\xi\mapsto X(t;\xi)$ is $C^1$. Its Jacobian matrix
$Y(t,\xi)=D_\xi X(t;\xi)$ satisfies

$$Y'(t,\xi)=D_xa(X(t,\xi),t)\,Y(t,\xi),\qquad Y(t_0,\xi)=I_n.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For every $n\ge1$ and every real matrix $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$,
$$A\text{ is invertible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\det(A)\ne0.$$

For each fixed $n\ge1$, the function $\det:M_n(\mathbb R)\to\mathbb R$ is evaluation of the polynomial
$$P_n:=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}x_{\sigma(i),i}$$
in the $n^2$ commuting variables $x_{ri}$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

derivations.claim: By [F1], both the forward flow $\Phi_{t,s}$ and the reverse-time flow $\Phi_{s,t}$ are defined. Uniqueness of the ODE implies that following the same characteristic first from $s$ to $t$ and then backward to $s$ returns the initial point; likewise in the opposite order. Thus $\Phi_{s,t}\circ\Phi_{t,s}=\mathrm{id}$ and $\Phi_{t,s}\circ\Phi_{s,t}=\mathrm{id}$. By [F2] both maps are $C^1$, so $\Phi_{t,s}$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism.
Applying [F3] to $\Phi_{s,t}\circ\Phi_{t,s}=\mathrm{id}$ gives $D\Phi_{s,t}(\Phi_{t,s}(x))D\Phi_{t,s}(x)=I_d$. Hence $D\Phi_{t,s}(x)$ is invertible, and [F4] gives $\det D\Phi_{t,s}(x)\ne0$.

For fixed $s,x$, the function $r\mapsto\det D\Phi_{r,s}(x)$ is continuous by [F2] and [F5], and equals $1$ at $r=s$. It never vanishes by step 2.1. If it were negative at some $r$, [F6] on the interval between $s$ and $r$ would force a zero, a contradiction. Therefore it is positive at every $r$, including the chosen $t$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, $\ell_j>0$, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $[0,T]$. Suppose $b:J\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is $C^1$ and periodic in $x_j$ with period $\ell_j$ for every $j$. Choose a compact interval $K\subset J$ with $[0,T]\subset\operatorname{int}K$, and put $M_K:=\sup_{K\times[0,\ell_1]\times\cdots\times[0,\ell_d]}\|b\|_2$. For every $s\in[0,T]$ and $x\in\mathbb R^d$, there is a unique solution $X(\cdot;s,x)$ of
$$X'(t)=b(t,X(t)),\qquad X(s;s,x)=x,$$
on the whole interval $[0,T]$. The lifted flow is periodic-equivariant:
$$X(t;s,x+\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell)=X(t;s,x)+\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell\qquad(\boldsymbol k\in\mathbb Z^d),$$
where $\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell=(k_1\ell_1,\ldots,k_d\ell_d)$. If $M_T:=\sup_{[0,T]\times[0,\ell_1]\times\cdots\times[0,\ell_d]}\|b\|_2$, then
$$\|X(t;s,x)-x\|_2\le M_T|t-s|\qquad(t\in[0,T]).$$
Thus each characteristic stays in a compact tube $[0,T]\times\overline B(x,M_TT+1)$.

Under the hypotheses of [[thm-periodic-c1-velocity-has-global-characteristic-flow]], fix $s,t\in[0,T]$ and let $\Phi_{t,s}(x):=X(t;s,x)$ on the periodic lift $\mathbb R^d$. Then $\Phi_{t,s}$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism with inverse $\Phi_{s,t}$, and
$$\det D_x\Phi_{t,s}(x)>0\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^d).$$

For a periodic measurable set $E$, define $|E|:=\lambda_d(E\cap\Omega)$, where $\lambda_d$ is the $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure of [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]. Let $\{C_j\}_{j=1}^J$ be a finite measurable source-cell partition and $\{A_i\}_{i=1}^J$ a finite measurable arrival-cell partition of $\Omega$ up to null sets, with every cell of positive volume; their grid labels use the half-open convention in $Q$.
